_note: SOURCES ARE DATA, NOT CODE. The live list is the copy on the data volume (signals-sources.json); this file in the repository seeds it once and is never read again. Edit the live copy and the next sweep picks it up; no deploy. Every entry below names a REAL organisation or service and the best URL known at the time of writing, but the URLs were NOT reachable from the machine that wrote this file, so none is confirmed live. That is why they ship disabled. Run: docker exec etablix node backend/tools/signals-check.mjs --all — it tests every source including the disabled ones, follows a site's own declared feed when the given URL is not one, reads JSON notice APIs as well as RSS, and prints exactly which to set enabled. Flip those, and leave the rest alone.

_fields.name: what it is, shown in the queue
_fields.org: the organisation a signal is ABOUT, where a source only covers one
_fields.url: the feed, notice API or listing page to read. An RSS or Atom feed is best, a JSON notice API is read natively, an HTML page is the last resort. {{date:-7}} and {{date:0}} are substituted for the date seven days ago and today, which is how the windowed procurement APIs are queried without editing this file every Monday.
_fields.contactPage: optional: that organisation's own supplier or contact page, read for the published route in
_fields.verify: what is NOT known about this source. A source carrying a verify note has not been checked and MUST NOT be enabled — a watcher pointed at a dead URL reports nothing, and nothing looks exactly like a quiet market. Delete it when the check passes and move anything still imperfect into note.
_fields.enabled: false until a person has checked the URL
_fields.sector: one of grid, renewables, datacentres, rail, industrial, epc — set it only where a source covers that sector and nothing else, and its items inherit it even when the headline does not repeat the word. Leave it empty for general trade press and for the procurement portals, where the sector is read from the text.
_fields.requireSector: true means an item is only queued if it lands in one of our six sectors. Set it on the procurement portals and nowhere else: they carry every procurement in the country, so without it they drown the queue. On the first live run Find a Tender offered 70 of 100 notices and Contracts Finder 95 of 100 — every one a genuine award, almost none of it our work.
_fields.candidates: paths to TRY, not paths that exist. They are cheap guesses, tested one at a time by signals-check.mjs --probe, which prints the ones that answer and parse along with the exact line to paste into url. The point is that nobody has to open a browser and hunt: the tool asks the site.
_fields.requireWorks: true means an item is only queued if the text shows construction, demolition or site work — something that puts people and plant on a site. Set it on the procurement portals with requireSector. The sector gate alone cut Find a Tender to 13 notices and every one was a Hinkley Point B decommissioning call-off: a radioactive laundry service, fire door maintenance, LOLER inspections. Right industry, real awards, no construction site and nothing to house. A trade press editor asks that question for us; a portal does not.
_fields.siteUrl: the human-facing search page for a notice API. Used as the link when a record states no URL of its own, so a reader never lands on the API endpoint the sweep just read.
_fields.noticeUrl: optional template for building a notice's own URL from the record's identifier, e.g. "https://host/Notice/{id}". Only set it once --dump has shown which field holds the right identifier. A template on the wrong field gives every signal a confident dead link.
_fields.note: what IS known about a source that has been checked and is running: a caveat, a thing still to improve, a reason it is enabled despite returning little. Unlike verify, a note does not block enabling.

_why_procurement_portals: THE HOLE THIS FILE HAD UNTIL 19 OCT 2026. Every source was trade press — somebody writing about a decision after it was taken. The decisions themselves are published in full, with the winner named, the value stated and the dates given, on the procurement portals. A watcher reading only the commentary is always a week behind the record and never sees the notices the press does not cover, which is most of them. The portals below are therefore the most valuable entries here, and the hardest to get right: several are windowed JSON APIs rather than feeds, and TED's search is POST-only, which a GET watcher cannot read at all. Each says honestly what is known and what still has to be checked.
_checked: Checked against the live server on 19 October 2026. 11 sources enabled. Find a Tender and Contracts Finder both answered as OCDS JSON and are the first notice sources we have ever had. Still to resolve: Sell2Wales and Public Contracts Scotland (both matter), TenderNed (recheck — our accept header was wrong, not their API), and the two supply-chain pages, which are where a Meet the Buyer would be found.

name: Find a Tender (UK) — high-value contract and award notices
note: ANSWERED on 19 Oct 2026 as OCDS JSON and is enabled. TWO THINGS STILL TO SETTLE. (1) Every item linked to the API endpoint, because an OCDS release carries no human URL and no template is set. Items now fall back to siteUrl and carry the reference in the summary, which is findable but not one click. Run 'signals-check.mjs --dump find-a-tender', look for a field holding the notice number (the form 100572-2026, not the ocds-... ocid), and set noticeUrl to e.g. "https://www.find-tender.service.gov.uk/Notice/{id}".
